newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Illicit weapons widespread in Zaire - U.N. report.
newsitem.headline: Illicit weapons widespread in Zaire - U.N. report.

text.p: Rwandan Hutu rebels in eastern Zaire have been amply supplied with arms from Europe and South Africa, with organisers of the illicit traffic based in Kenya, said a U.N. report obtained on Tuesday.

The report prepared for the U.N. Security Council by a four-man U.N.-appointed Commission of Inquiry is part of a series documenting violations of an arms embargo imposed after the 1994 ethnic massacres against Tutsis in Rwanda.
Zairean complicity in the deals ranked high in all the past and current reports from the commission, obtained by Reuters.

The commission also sought to trace the origin of weapons, the arms dealers, or the transit points through a number of countries including Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Britain, Italy, Belgium, Spain and Malta.
Money was raised through Hutus based in Kenya, through counterfeit U.S. dollar printing presses and other means in an effort to stoke the civil war in Rwanda, the report said.
In addition, "war taxes" were imposed on refugees employed by international aid agencies and some relief goods were sold.
After the 1994 Rwanda killings that left more than 500,000 people dead, mostly minority Tutsis, a million Hutus fled to eastern Zaire, including soldiers and militia.

The crisis escalated recently when ethnic Tutsis in Zaire fought the Zairean army with the refugees caught in the crossfire. With world leaders calling for aid to the refugees, the commissioners raised doubts about reconstituting the same Hutu camps near Goma in eastern Zaire.

"Reliable and highly reliable sources in Belgium, Kenya, Rwanda, South Africa, Tanzania and the United Kingdom painted a coherent picture of huge, loose, overlapping webs or more or less illicit arms deals, arms flights and arms deliveries spanning the continent from South Africa as far as Europe, particularly eastern Europe," said the report.
Zaire's airport in Kinshasa, the capital, appeared to serve as a "hub for weapons shipments," the report said.

Leaders of the Rwandan former military, including army chief Gen. Augustin Bizimungu, held regular meetings in Kenyan hotels to organise the effort that the commission believes included getting funds from a Nairobi-based printing press for counterfeit U.S. dollars.
All the Rwandans under suspicion in Kenya are travelling on passports from Zaire, the commission said.
Their aim, the report said, apparently was to invade Rwanda and at minimum to identify witnesses to the genocide who might testify on war crimes before the U.N. tribunal on Rwanda.

"The commission was given a detailed description of the ways in which genocide survivors or those who might give evidence ... are identified, tracked and killed, even if they are in the custody of the Rwandan goverment," the report said.
But it said both Zairean and Kenyan leaders had ignored requests for more information or investigations.
Among other reports the commission was looking into and awaiting responses from the governments were:
-- More details on its earlier report tracing South African weapons to the Seychelles en route to Zaire with money passing through Geneva's Union Bancaire Privee.
-- An unidentified British-based company alleged to have been involved in transporting arms to Goma.
-- 50 anti-personnel mines manufactured in southern Italy.
-- Inquiries on two Ukrainian-registered planes with 30 tons of arms landing in Egypt enroute from Bulgaria to Zaire.
-- Meetings between a French national, who has since disappeared, and General Bizimungu in Zaire.
-- A Nigerian-registered plane with suspected arms stopping in Spain and Malta enroute to Goma in eastern Zaire.
-- Approaches to arms industries in the Czech Republic.
-- Arms deliveries from Zambia across Lake Tanganyika.
-- An inquiry in Belgium on possible false documents for the destination or origin of weapons.
